label: Start
title: What I am looking for
promise: Before you look at any place, write down what you are measuring it against.
intro_title: Why the measuring stick comes first
intro: Once you start looking at places, it is easy to let them change what you said you needed. Photographs show them at their best. Advertised prices do not include every cost. A June visit tells you little about life there in February.
Write down what you need before you start looking. Then compare every place against the same list. You'll notice if you start changing your requirements because you prefer a certain place.
This page takes twenty minutes, and you use it in every part that follows.
route_title: Write down what you are looking for
talk: If you are moving with someone, each of you should complete this page separately. Then compare and talk about where your answers differ. Have that conversation now, before you arrive.

finish.title: What I Am Looking For
finish.description: The measuring stick you use for every place in this step.

example.text: What matters most: (1) I can grow food at least eight months a year, (2) a hospital within 45 minutes because of my daughter, (3) internet good enough for video calls, because my income comes from clients abroad. Nice but not essential: near the sea.

label: Part 1
title: Which country?
promise: Ten honest questions that separate a place you like in theory from a place where your life can work.
can_skip: If you have chosen your country and answered the friendly challenge under "Where do you start?", go to Part 2. You can return here if your research in Part 3 uncovers a barrier, such as not being allowed to live there.
intro_title: Start with the list, not the map
intro: When I chose a country, I began with a list of what my life needed. Then I checked which countries fitted. It sounds obvious, but it is easy to start with somewhere you already like and try to make it work.
A list gives you something to score, compare and check. Your feeling about a country matters too, and you will explore that in Part 4. This part helps you decide which places are worth visiting.
The ten factors below give you a starting point. I used the first eight myself and added the last two later, because I have seen how often they stop a plan.

finish.title: My Country Choice
finish.description: One country to explore, with your reasons and your open questions.

exercises.title: The ten factors

rows: 1. Climate and nature
Look at the whole year. How hot, cold, wet or dry does it get? Is there enough water? How do you cope with that climate?
2. What your plan needs
Land, space, a workshop, clients, a job, a school, a studio, quiet. What does your picture from Step 1 physically need?
3. The rules
What are you allowed to do there? Build, renovate, work from home, keep animals, live off-grid, run a business, work as a foreigner.
4. Support and costs from the state

Some countries offer support for newcomers or particular plans; others make the process expensive or slow. Taxes and support change, so check any figure you find on a forum against an official source.
5. Community and language
Can you connect with people? People doing something similar? How hard is the local language for you, and how much will you need it?
6. Amenities and healthcare
Distance to a doctor, hospital, pharmacy, shops, and schools. What does healthcare cost, and who is allowed to use it?
7. Your budget
What can you afford to buy or rent, and what will daily life cost? A place that fits your budget gives you more time to settle in.
8. Infrastructure
Roads, electricity, water, internet, public transport, deliveries. Can you actually work and live there?
9. Your legal right to live there
Can you get permission to stay? What do you have to prove: income, savings, insurance, work? How long does it take?
10. Distance to the people you love
Flights, cost, travel time. And a harder question: if someone close to you becomes ill, how quickly could you reach them?

tips: Factors 3, 4, 6 and 9 involve rules that change. Use official government sources, record the date you checked, and check again before deciding. Part 3 shows you how.

exercises.title: Score your countries
intro: Scoring helps you see your reasons clearly. It shows which countries fall short on something important and where you still need information. The highest total is not necessarily the right choice.

start_here.prompt: Choose two to four countries you are curious about. Thinking of staying? Include your own country. Score each factor: 2 = good for me, 1 = maybe, 0 = no. Leave a box empty if you do not know yet, and add it to your research list.

row_labels: 4. Support and costs from the state

exercises.challenge: Look at the zeros before the total. A zero on a must-have rules a country out, no matter how high it scores elsewhere. Then look at the empty boxes: those tell you what to research next.

story.text: As Bali became busier, I missed working with my hands and growing things. A YouTube channel about self-sufficient living helped me see what I wanted next. I listed what that life needed: climate and soil, water, land-use rules, off-grid living, nearby healthcare, an affordable place to live, and the infrastructure to stay connected. I compared five countries: Portugal, New Zealand, Costa Rica, Australia and Canada. Portugal fitted best.

exercises.title: The two questions that end most plans
intro: Two questions can stop an otherwise appealing plan. They are easy to leave until the end, but they need answers early.

Am I allowed to live there? Every country sets its own conditions for who can stay and for how long. Your passport, income, work and family situation all matter. Someone else's experience doesn't determine what applies to you.

Can I afford to live there? Compare the cost of an ordinary month with your First Money Picture from Step 1. Include housing, food, energy, healthcare, transport, insurance, and something for enjoyment. A holiday budget will not answer this question.

start_here.prompt: Write what you know about your situation today. Use "unknown" where you still need an answer. It gives you something clear to investigate.

fields.label: Am I allowed to live there? What I know today
What I would have to prove
Can I afford a normal month there? What I know today
What I still need to find out, and where

where_to_check: Rules about living in a country come from that country's government, not from a blog or me. For Portugal, the official pages are gov.pt (theme: foreigners in Portugal), aima.gov.pt (residence), and vistos.mne.gov.pt (visas). Other countries have similar official pages. Write the date you checked next to every answer.
exercises.expert_work: Take questions about tax, residence law, pensions and investments to a qualified adviser in the country concerned. The answers depend on your circumstances. Use this workbook to prepare the questions you need to ask.

go_deeper.prompt: Take your best country and argue against it for ten minutes. What is the strongest reason not to go there? Write it down. If you cannot find one, you have not looked hard enough yet.

summary.title: What does this tell me?
summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: Which country fits most of my ten factors?
Where are my zeros, and are they on a must-have?
What do I still not know, and where can I find it?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Country Choice. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: The country I want to explore further
Two or three reasons why
Countries I let go of, and why
My biggest doubt about this country
What I must check before I decide, and where

example.text: Country: Portugal. Why: I feel well in that climate, my money goes further than at home, and I work online, so I need reliable internet. I ruled out Costa Rica because it is too far from my parents and flights are expensive. My biggest doubt is winter in a stone house. I need to find out how people heat their homes and what it costs.

summary.result: My Country Choice — one country to explore, with your reasons and your open questions.

staying: Do this part anyway, with your own country in it. Score it like any other, next to one or two countries that have crossed your mind. If your own country still comes out best, you have checked it instead of assuming it. That is a strong reason to stay.

label: Part 2
title: Which region?
promise: A country is not one place. Inside one country, life can be completely different from one valley to the next.
can_skip: If you have chosen a region and answered the friendly challenge under "Where do you start?", go to Part 3. Read the ten region questions first, though. It takes two minutes and can bring up something you haven't considered.
intro_title: The region decides your daily life
intro: Once you have chosen a country, it is tempting to visit the best-known region and buy there. Take time to compare it with other areas before spending money.
Your country decides your paperwork. Your region shapes your daily life: the weather, neighbours, costs, the journey to the hospital, internet, and how busy or quiet it is in August and January.

Keep two or three regions on your list long enough to compare them properly. A second visit elsewhere helps you notice what you missed the first time. By the third, you will have a clearer sense of what matters to you.
talk: Find two or three people who actually live in the regions on your list, in online groups or through people you know. Ask them one question: "What do you wish you had known before you moved here?" The answer is usually not in any brochure.

finish.title: My Region Shortlist
finish.description: Two or three regions, with what you like and what worries you.

rows: 1. Climate through the year
Summer heat, winter cold, rain, wind, fog, snow. In one country, you can find all of them.
2. Land and nature
Flat land or mountains, forest or open ground, soil, water, and the risk of fire or flooding.
3. What things cost
Houses, land, rent. Within one country, prices can differ by three or four times.
4. Distance to care
How far is it to a doctor, a hospital, a pharmacy? How long does an ambulance take?
5. Daily needs
Shops, schools, sports, banks, post offices, fuel. How far would you travel for everyday needs?
6. Work and income
Jobs, clients, tourists, seasons. Or can you bring your income with you?
7. Getting in and out
Airport, train, motorway. How easy is it for you to leave, and for people to visit?
8. Internet and mobile
Check the speed at a specific address on an ordinary evening, rather than simply asking whether internet is available.
9. People and language
Who lives there? Are there other newcomers? How much of the local language will you need?
10. Busy and quiet
Some places are packed in summer and empty in winter. Would both seasons suit you?

exercises.title: Portugal: the map in simple words
intro: This section focuses on Portugal. If you are considering another country, use the same questions to understand its regions.

Mainland Portugal is divided into 18 districts, plus the two island regions, Madeira and the Azores. For statistics, the mainland is often grouped into five regions: North, Centre, Lisbon area, Alentejo and Algarve.

The weather is not the same everywhere, and the differences are bigger than most people expect for a small country. The national weather institute, IPMA, classifies the climate of the mainland like this:

rows: Most of the mainland
Temperate, with a dry summer
Inland Douro valley (part of Bragança district) and most areas south of the Montejunto–Estrela mountain line
Warm, dry summers (climate type Csa)
Almost all areas north of that mountain line, plus the west coast of Alentejo and the Algarve
Milder, dry summers (climate type Csb)
A small area in the Beja district, in the Alentejo
Dry steppe climate (type BSk)
Madeira
Warm, dry summers (Csa)
Azores
Eastern islands: mild, dry summers (Csb). Central and western islands: ocean climate, wetter all year (Cfb)

tables.lead: Beyond the weather: what else changes from region to region. Weather is often the first difference you notice. These four areas also vary between municipalities and can surprise newcomers. For now, know which questions to ask. A more detailed Portugal module, planned for later, will cover each one.
rows: Land and building rules

Every municipality has its own plan, the PDM (Plano Diretor Municipal), that says what may be built where. Land is usually classed as rústico (rural) or urbano (urban). On rural land, building a new house is often not allowed. These rules have changed recently, so check the current situation for the exact plot before you fall for it.
Fire risk
Large parts of the interior have a high fire risk. Owners must keep the land around houses clear of vegetation, and this is checked. Ask what it means for the place you look at, in work and in cost.
Water
Mains water does not reach everywhere. In the countryside, many homes use a well or a borehole, and these may need permission or registration with the environment agency.
Support and demand

Lisbon, Porto, the coast and the Algarve cost much more than the interior. The interior is cheaper, and programmes sometimes support people who move there. Those programmes change, so check what is current.

where_to_check: IPMA, Climate normals and climate classification, ipma.pt (checked 20 September 2026). IPMA also publishes average temperature and rainfall per month for weather stations across the country, for the periods 1971–2000, 1981–2010 and 1991–2020. Look up the station closest to the place you are considering, and look at the winter months, not only the summer ones.

Building and land-use rules are set locally. Start with the town or municipal council where the place is: its website, or its planning office. Most countries also have a national website that publishes the local plans. Ask the council, or a local fire service or forestry office, whether there is a fire risk and whether owners have to clear land. For water, find out whether mains water reaches the address. If not, check whether a well or borehole needs a permit and who issues it; this is usually the national or regional environment agency. Write down the source and the date you checked. In Portugal: the câmara municipal and pcgt.dgterritorio.gov.pt (land use), sgifr.gov.pt (fire safety) and apambiente.pt (wells and boreholes). Checked 27 September 2026.
tips: Inland and higher up means hotter summers and colder winters. Near the ocean means milder, but also windier and damper. Many older houses here were built for summer heat rather than winter cold, so before you fall in love with a house, find out how it works in every season: how it is heated in winter, and how it stays cool in summer.

start_here.prompt: Choose two to four regions. Thinking of staying? Include the region where you live now. Score each factor: 2 = good for me, 1 = maybe, 0 = no. Leave a box empty if you do not know yet, and add it to your research list.

story.text: I live near the Serra da Estrela mountains, in the district of Guarda. Coming from Bali, I didn't want a tropical climate. I wanted real seasons, but not a Northern European climate either. That brought me to central Portugal: far enough from the sea to avoid the wind, with mountains nearby, more rain, and summers less hot than, for example, in the Alentejo. There is also room to grow food. When I was searching, my budget was at most €100,000 for 2 to 3 hectares. Climate mattered just as much as price, so I looked mainly around Viseu, Guarda and Setúbal. In the end, central Portugal was the best fit. Your list will depend on your own needs. Keeping two or three regions open long enough to compare them helped me choose.

example.text: Region 1 scores well on price and nature, but the hospital is 50 minutes away. Region 2 costs more and has everything nearby. I am keeping both for now. On my test visit, I will find out how that drive feels in winter rain, rather than judging it on a sunny June day.

summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: Which two or three regions stay on my list?
What makes them different from each other?
What would make me drop one of them?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Region Shortlist. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: My shortlist: two or three regions
What attracts me in each one
What worries me in each one
Regions I let go, and why
What I must find out about each (Part 3)

summary.result: My Region Shortlist — two or three regions, with what you like and what worries you.

staying: Is the region where you live now still the best place for your picture? Score it as Region 1, next to one or two other regions in your own country. Sometimes the change you need isn't a new country, but a move an hour away: closer to nature, family, or work you enjoy.
